passage: On the grass in a Berlin park Kaito, two, was smashing a cracker in his fist. He walked over to his mother Clara, held out a damp crumbly piece, and said "Mama." "Oh, for me? Thank you, Kaito," said Clara, and pretended to nibble. He beamed. Later another toddler reached for his toy truck and Kaito pulled it in. Clara said only, "That's your truck. You can keep it," and let him be.

qa.q: What did Kaito hand to Clara?
qa.a: He handed her a damp, crumbly piece of cracker.

qa.q: What does Kaito's beaming suggest he was feeling, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It suggests he was pleased that his mother accepted his gift and liked sharing with her. It could also be that he enjoyed her attention.

qa.q: What did Clara do well with the truck moment?
qa.a: She did not force him to share, so his kindness with the cracker stayed his own choice. 🙂

qa.q: How might the other toddler feel when the truck was pulled away?
qa.a: The other toddler may feel disappointed for a moment, and they too are still learning about sharing.

grounding: A toddler offers food spontaneously, and a warm response reinforces kindness without forcing it.

passage: Akash was at his sister's house for lunch when Jahnavi, two, walked round the table with a piece of roti held out in her fist. She stopped in front of a guest and said, "Ta." The guest laughed, took a small bite, and thanked her. Jahnavi grinned and went back to her chair. Akash wondered if she was copying what she sees at meals; he could not tell.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi hold out to the guest?
qa.a: She held out a piece of roti.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's grin after the guest's bite suggest, and what else might explain her offer?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed sharing and the guest's warm reaction. Akash thinks she may just be copying what she sees at meals.

qa.q: How could adults respond to a toddler's offer like this?
qa.a: They can take it warmly, say thanks, and not push the child to offer again.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel if the guest had ignored her?
qa.a: She might feel puzzled or a little hurt, and be less likely to offer again.

grounding: A toddler spontaneously offers food to show sharing and social interest, and warm response reinforces it.

passage:
Sunday: Mahima held out her soggy biscuit to Varun. He pretended to take a bite. "Mmm! Thank you, Mahima." She laughed and ate the rest.
Wednesday: her cousin was crying on the rug. Mahima toddled over and held out her own doll. The cousin took it and stopped crying.
The next Saturday: Varun sat eating a banana. Mahima watched, then went and brought him her toy cup, holding it out with a smile.

qa.q: What did Mahima offer her crying cousin?
qa.a: Her own doll.

qa.q: What might Mahima have been feeling when she brought Varun her toy cup?
qa.a: She seemed friendly and happy to share, wanting to join in with him; offering the cup was a warm, spontaneous gesture.

qa.q: What could Varun do to encourage Mahima's offers?
qa.a: Keep responding warmly, taking the offer and thanking her, without forcing her to share.

qa.q: How might the cousin experience being handed the doll?
qa.a: The cousin probably felt comforted and a bit surprised by the kindness.

grounding: Over a week a toddler spontaneously offers food and toys, and warm responses encourage her kindness.

passage:
In the Kolkata park, Sonali toddled up to the bench where an older woman, Parul, sat with her newspaper. Sonali held out a pebble on her palm.
"Don't bother Aunty," her mother called.
"She's not bothering me," said Parul, putting her paper down. She took the pebble carefully. "For me? Thank you!" Sonali beamed, ran off and came back with a leaf.

qa.q: What was Parul reading?
qa.a: Her newspaper.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she held out the pebble?
qa.a: She was curious and friendly, wanting to share and connect with Parul; her beam shows she was delighted when it was accepted.

qa.q: Which of Parul's choices encouraged Sonali, and why?
qa.a: Putting the paper down and thanking her warmly encouraged Sonali, because her kindness was welcomed.

qa.q: How does Sonali's mother see the offer at first?
qa.a: She worries Sonali is bothering the stranger, not seeing it as a friendly gesture.

grounding: A toddler offers a stranger a pebble, and a warm response reinforces her spontaneous sharing.

passage:
"Santosh, give your car to your cousin. Share!" said Dadi.
Santosh clutched the car to his chest.
"Don't force it, Amma," said Uday, his father. "Let's wait."
A few minutes later, Santosh toddled over to his cousin, looked at him, and held out his ball.
"Oh! Thank you, Santosh!" said Uday. "That was kind."
Santosh ran back and fetched the car too.

qa.q: What did Santosh first offer his cousin?
qa.a: His ball.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he clutched the car?
qa.a: He felt protective of his car and didn't want it taken; once no one pushed him, he felt free to share on his own.

qa.q: Why was Uday's approach better than Dadi's?
qa.a: Waiting let Santosh offer freely, and Uday's warm thanks made him want to share more, while forcing only made him hold on tighter.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Santosh offers the ball and then the car?
qa.a: The cousin would likely feel happy and included. 😊

grounding: A father waits instead of forcing sharing, and his toddler makes a spontaneous offer that is warmly thanked.

passage:
Playgroup note, Thursday. From Tushar, helper.
At snack time Pradeep held out his half-eaten biscuit to me, soggy, with a big smile. I said, “For me? Thank you!” and pretended to munch. He laughed.
Later he pushed his toy car into another child's hands, all by himself.
A few minutes later he wanted it back and cried. I didn't make him share; I helped the other child find a truck.

qa.q: What did Pradeep hold out at snack time?
qa.a: His half-eaten biscuit.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he offered his biscuit?
qa.a: He seemed happy and friendly, sharing on the spur of the moment to connect with Tushar; the big smile shows it was a pleasure to give.

qa.q: Why did Tushar not make Pradeep share the car again?
qa.a: Forcing sharing would take the joy out of it; warmly thanking his spontaneous offers encourages kindness better.

qa.q: How might the other child have felt when Pradeep gave the car?
qa.a: The other child was probably surprised and pleased, and then disappointed when Pradeep wanted it back.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler spontaneously offering food and a toy, and an adult responding warmly without forcing sharing.
